title: ⭐⭐ Practice: the pronoun that comes back, and the advice that arrives in time

questions.prompt: A pupil writes in her diary: "The exam is on Monday and I have not opened the book. I ……… start tonight." She means that if she does not start tonight, things will go badly. Which form says that?

options.text: have better
needn't
hadn't better
had better

questions.explanation: had better is the urgent one of the three advice forms: it does not simply say that an action is wise, it hints at the bad consequence of not doing it, which is exactly the situation the diary describes. needn't says the opposite of what she means, since it declares an action pointless. The negative of this form is had better not, placed after had better, so hadn't better is not English at all. And the form is built on had for every person, however present the meaning is — it is usually shortened to 'd better, which is why so many pupils drop the word altogether and write you better.

questions.prompt: In the examination room, Paul says he is not sure of two answers and has no time left to check them. Mary says the test is easy and she won't bother checking hers. Both complaints are about checking. Which advice belongs to Mary?

options.text: Always leave yourself enough time at the end to check all your answers.
Keep calm; if you've done your revision, there's no need to panic.
Use all the time you have; if you finish early, check everything again.
Don't waste time on one question; leave it and come back later.

questions.explanation: Mary's problem is not a shortage of time but a refusal to use the time she has, so the advice that fits her is the one about finishing early and going back over everything, even the easy questions. Leaving enough time to check belongs to Paul instead: he wants to check and cannot, which is the mirror image of Mary's case and the reason the two are printed together. Keeping calm answers Andy, whose mind has gone blank although he revised. And not wasting time on one question answers Beth, who has spent ten minutes on a single item — a pupil who is stuck, not one who is idle.

questions.prompt: Read this line from a school report: "Mr Bean looks anxious. He must be worried about his sick mother." What is must doing here?

options.text: Ordering Mr Bean to worry.
Drawing a conclusion from the evidence.
Advising Mr Bean to go and see his sick mother.
Saying that worrying is forbidden.

questions.explanation: The first sentence supplies evidence — the anxious look — and the second states what the writer concludes from it. That is the deduction use of must, where the modal measures how sure the speaker is rather than what anybody has to do. Nobody can be ordered to worry, and no order is addressed to Mr Bean anywhere in the two sentences; the writer is talking about him, not to him. Nor is it advice, which would need should, ought to or had better and would concern something still to be decided. And a prohibition would take mustn't, which is not the same word doing a different job but a different meaning altogether.

options.text: The children look after theirselves while their parents are away.
The children look after themself while their parents are away.
The children are looking after theirself while their parents are away.
The children look after themselves while their parents are away.

questions.explanation: The third person plural reflexive is themselves: the object pronoun them plus the plural ending -selves. theirselves is built on the possessive their, which the third person never uses for its reflexive — that pattern belongs to myself and yourself alone. themself keeps the singular ending on a plural subject, and the children are several, so the ending has to be -selves. And theirself makes both mistakes at once, the possessive stem and the singular ending, which is why it is the form learners reach for when they are guessing rather than remembering.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes: "My brother took the exam in June and passed it." Another writes: "My brother passed the exam room and went in." Only one of them is using pass with its ordinary English meaning. What does to pass an exam mean?

options.text: To succeed in it.
To be present at it.
To walk past the room where it is held.
To spend time doing it.

questions.explanation: to pass an exam means to succeed in it, and its opposite is to fail. That is why the first pupil's sentence works: he took the exam, which says he sat it, and then passed it, which says he got through. Being present at an exam is what to sit or to take an exam says, and English keeps that quite separate — a pupil who took the exam may very well have failed it. Walking past the room is the everyday meaning of pass followed by a place, which is what makes the second pupil's sentence odd rather than wrong. And spending time doing something would be to spend, or to pass the time, which needs the word time to work.

questions.prompt: A teacher writes on the board three sentences of advice and asks which one is wrongly built. Which is it?

options.text: You should plan your time before you begin.
You ought to read the whole paper once.
You had better to check your answers.
You had better not leave it to the last minute.

questions.explanation: had better is followed by the base verb with no to, so the correct form is you had better check. Of the three advice forms, only ought keeps to, which is why reading the whole paper once is properly built. should takes the base verb directly as well, so planning your time before you begin is right. And the negative places not immediately after had better and keeps the base verb, which is what the last sentence does — a form worth noticing, because the temptation is to write hadn't better, which does not exist.
